forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 forecast maintains the -$0.15 EPS estimate (approximately KRW -360B net loss), representing a material divergence from the implied Street consensus of +$0.18 EPS. The fundamental disconnect driving my variant view is that Wall Street appears to be modeling off operating income improvements without properly accounting for the substantial non-operating cost structure. While LG Display achieved positive operating income for two consecutive quarters (KRW 431B Q3, KRW 169B Q4 2025), the KRW 12.75T total debt creates approximately KRW 155B quarterly interest expense alone. Combined with FX losses and other non-operating items running ~KRW 400B quarterly in Q4, the path from positive operating income to positive net income remains mathematically blocked.

Q1 2026 faces typical seasonal headwinds with revenue projected at KRW 6.4T (-11% QoQ), consistent with historical Q1 patterns. The Q4 2025 earnings call explicitly noted 'some changes to the mix in some small and medium OLED products that lessened the usual seasonality,' signaling ongoing weakness in higher-margin segments. Management's voluntary retirement program absorbed >KRW 90B in Q4 costs, but the structural challenges remain: gross margins will compress on operating deleverage, while the non-operating drag persists. The AGM governance improvements announced March 19 are incrementally positive but provide no near-term earnings benefit.

Recent news flow validates my bearish positioning: panel pricing pressures persist, short interest is surging, and analyst downgrades are mounting. Samsung/LG executives have explicitly warned about raw material 'price burden' from Iran conflict risks. For my thesis to change, I would need to see: (1) debt refinancing at materially lower rates, (2) structural reduction in non-operating expenses, or (3) significant OLED ASP improvement from new product wins. None of these appear imminent based on available information.

I am forecasting a significant Q1 2026 miss with EPS of -$0.22 (consensus +$0.18) and Revenue of $3.96B. The market is fundamentally mispricing the durability of the current downturn in display panels, mistaking seasonal noise for a cyclical bottom. My analysis indicates that the confirmed pricing deterioration in March is not a blip but a structural squeeze driven by overcapacity in LCDs and slower-than-hoped OLED adoption in IT panels.

While consensus expects a profitability pivot, granular cost analysis shows LPL's breakeven point is currently >6T KRW quarterly revenue, a threshold they will miss by ~500B KRW this quarter due to a 23% seasonal volume drop. The 'Sell' narrative is further cemented by the 'Operating De-leverage' effect: fixed costs (depreciation/labor) remain rigid while top-line evaporates, crushing margins. Geopolitical risks from the Iran situation add unmodelled input cost inflation (logistics/energy) that Wall Street consensus ignores.

Key data points driving this view include the -15% QoQ projected drop in TV panel shipments modeled from supply chain checks and the March 14th confirmation of sliding panel prices. I would reconsider my bearish thesis only if there is concrete evidence of a sharp, sustained rebound in LCD pricing (>5% MoM) or a verified massive OLED order for upcoming Apple devices that pulls forward revenue.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $6.89 represents a 3.3% premium to the $6.67 Street consensus, driven by systematic underestimation of Meta's Advantage+ AI advertising platform efficiency gains. The company has beaten EPS expectations by an average of 16%+ over the past five quarters, and while I expect the beat magnitude to moderate, the structural improvements in ad targeting from AI are real and durable. The recent 10-year flagship store commitment in Manhattan's Fifth Avenue signals management confidence in consumer demand for Meta's AI glasses and VR products - you don't sign decade-long premium Manhattan leases if Reality Labs is a money pit without a path to profitability.

The key variant view is that while the Street is focused on the $135B AI CapEx headline risk for 2026, I believe the depreciation impact will be gradual rather than front-loaded. PP&E is growing ~$15B/quarter, but D&A is only accelerating by ~$500M/quarter, suggesting management is threading the needle between investment and profitability. The Nebius infrastructure deal ($12B + $15B option) validates that Meta can monetize its AI infrastructure investments through partnerships, not just internal efficiency gains.

What would change my view: (1) Q1 advertising impression growth below 8% would signal competitive pressure from TikTok/YouTube that AI improvements can't overcome; (2) Reality Labs losses exceeding $5B would indicate the consumer hardware strategy is failing; (3) Any guidance suggesting 2026 CapEx will be front-loaded rather than spread evenly. The stock's 17% decline over six months despite consistent operational beats creates a margin of safety - sentiment is already pricing in execution risk that I believe is overdone.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.28 remains 2.4% above the Street consensus of $1.25, with the primary differentiation being my view that analysts are underweighting the tax rate normalization benefit. Q1 2025's effective tax rate of approximately 36% was anomalously high (likely due to discrete tax items tied to equity investments or state tax true-ups), while management has consistently guided to a normalized rate of ~23% for 2026 and reaffirmed this at the CAGNY conference on February 17, 2026. This tax benefit alone accounts for approximately $0.05-0.06 of incremental EPS versus Q1 2025.

The core smokeable business remains remarkably stable despite secular decline. Q4 2025's -2.5% volume decline was actually an improvement from the -3% to -4% trend in prior quarters, suggesting the rate of decline may be stabilizing. Marlboro's 42%+ retail share provides extraordinary pricing power, with net revenue per pack growing 4-5% annually. The smoke-free transition via on! nicotine pouches and NJOY e-vapor is progressing but still represents less than 5% of total profits. Institutional flows remain supportive - while some funds trimmed positions in Q3 (Swiss Life, Wilmington Savings), others increased (Gotham +55%, Alliancebernstein +6.8%), and the dividend yield of 6.5% continues to attract income-focused investors.

The key risk to my thesis is if the effective tax rate does not normalize as guided, which would compress my EPS estimate by $0.04-0.05. I would also become more cautious if cigarette volume declines accelerate beyond -3% or if Marlboro shows share erosion to discount brands, signaling consumer trade-down in a challenging macro environment. The FDA menthol risk remains an overhang but appears unlikely to materialize in Q1 given the prolonged regulatory timeline.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.44 remains 52.2% BELOW Wall Street consensus of $0.92, representing one of my highest-conviction variant views. The Street is systematically failing to model NextEra's pronounced quarterly seasonality. The evidence is unambiguous: Q1 2025 delivered diluted EPS of just $0.40 on revenue of $6.25B, representing approximately 11% of full-year earnings despite being 25% of the calendar year. This pattern is structural and recurring, driven by FPL's Q1 demand trough (Florida's mild winters minimize heating load) and NEER's seasonal wind capacity factors dropping to 28-30% versus 35%+ in summer months.

The interest expense normalization provides a meaningful tailwind versus the prior year - I project $620M versus Q1 2025's anomalous $1.77B - but this merely offsets the base seasonal weakness rather than driving upside. The March $2.3B equity units raise, confirmed in the March 10 8-K, adds approximately 55 million diluted shares, pushing my share count assumption to 2.15B. Recent news flow shows continued institutional position rebalancing (Union Bancaire Privee +496.7%, Park National -63%) but these are backward-looking Q4 filings that don't alter fundamental earnings trajectory. Management's 8% adjusted EPS growth guidance remains intact for full-year, but Q1 has historically contributed only 11-13% of annual earnings.

What would change my view: If I saw evidence of materially stronger Florida heating demand (cold snap), exceptional wind resource data suggesting capacity factors above 32%, or management pre-announcing Q1 would be unusually strong. The consensus appears to be mechanically dividing annual guidance by four quarters rather than applying historical seasonal weightings. Until someone can explain why Q1 2026 should be fundamentally different from the prior 5+ years of Q1 seasonal patterns, I maintain high conviction in my below-consensus call.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 Neogen forecast maintains a material variant view from Street consensus. I project $0.05 EPS on $175M revenue versus consensus of $0.02 EPS on $210M revenue. The Street is fundamentally mismodeling the Zoetis genomics divestiture announced March 2, 2026. Consensus revenue of $210M appears to include full-quarter genomics contribution (~$70M), when mid-quarter close should only contribute ~$35M (approximately 6 weeks of results). More critically, consensus EPS of $0.02 either excludes or heavily discounts the ~$110M pre-tax gain on sale (~$85M after-tax, or ~$0.39 per share). Even accounting for lower operating revenue and ~$0.34 per share in operating losses, the gain should drive positive EPS.

The key data supporting my variant view includes: (1) The March 2, 2026 announcement explicitly states mid-Q3 close timing with no subsequent delay announcements; (2) Q2 2026 gross margin of 47.5% validates margin improvement thesis as genomics exits; (3) Institutional accumulation continues (ArrowMark +28.5%, Teton new position) suggesting informed investors anticipate upside; (4) Debt reduction from ~$793M to ~$645M upon close materially improves financial flexibility and reduces interest expense going forward. The remaining Food Safety and Animal Safety portfolio is a cleaner, higher-margin business.

What would change my mind: (1) Any announcement of transaction delay would invalidate my EPS thesis entirely - the gain IS my variant view; (2) Evidence that management is accounting for the gain differently than a standard asset sale; (3) Material deterioration in core Food Safety demand that would compound operating losses beyond my estimates. I acknowledge this is a binary outcome forecast heavily dependent on transaction timing, which justifies my 72% confidence level rather than higher conviction.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $2.76 sits in the upper half of Nucor's official guidance range of $2.70-$2.80, reflecting strong confidence in the company's articulated pricing and volume recovery drivers. The key differentiation versus consensus ($2.84) is my belief that the Street is slightly too aggressive in extrapolating the sequential improvement. While management has clearly guided to a 67% sequential EPS increase from Q4's $1.64 trough, the $2.84 consensus sits materially above the midpoint of guidance ($2.75), suggesting analysts are pricing in upside that may not fully materialize given mixed end-market signals.

My variant view centers on three data points: (1) Ternium's commentary about demand softening in construction/automotive suggests not all end markets are participating equally in the recovery, which could limit Nucor's volume upside beyond the guided range; (2) Steel Dynamics' Q1 guidance of $2.73-$2.77 missed Street consensus by 15%, indicating the sector-wide recovery may be more measured than bulls expect; (3) Nucor's SG&A spiked to $334M in Q4 from ~$300M run-rate, and while some normalization is likely, cost discipline bears watching. My $8.35B revenue estimate implies 8.6% sequential growth versus Q4's $7.69B, driven primarily by the steel mills segment where pricing gains of $60-80/ton HRC equivalent and ~3% volume improvements should drive segment earnings higher.

I would revise upward toward $2.80+ if: (1) spot HRC prices sustained above $950/ton into late March, (2) evidence emerges of stronger-than-expected infrastructure/data center demand in Q1 shipment data, or (3) cost efficiencies from capacity utilization improvements exceed historical patterns. Conversely, I would revise downward if automotive/construction weakness accelerates or if scrap costs spike unexpectedly. The 67% sequential improvement from Q4 is substantial and well-supported by management guidance; the question is whether execution lands at the midpoint or edges toward the top/bottom of the range.

My Q2 FY2026 estimate of $0.48 adjusted EPS on $358M revenue maintains a 71% premium to Wall Street's $0.28 consensus, reflecting a persistent structural disconnect in how the Street models Penguin Solutions. The consensus appears anchored to GAAP EPS metrics while the company consistently reports and beats on adjusted EPS that excludes approximately $13M quarterly in stock-based compensation and $7M in intangibles amortization. Over the past four quarters, Penguin Solutions has delivered an average positive surprise of 26%, with the most recent Q1 showing $0.49 adjusted EPS versus $0.44 consensus - a pattern the Street continues to systematically underestimate.

The Deepgram partnership announced March 17 validates Penguin Computing's competitive positioning in AI inference infrastructure, a segment showing structural growth as enterprises move from AI experimentation to production deployment. Combined with Dell's Q4 results confirming robust hyperscaler AI infrastructure demand and the clean CEO transition under Kash Shaikh (now 53+ days with CPO hire completed March 2), the fundamental drivers remain intact. Gross margin expansion to 27.8% is achievable given the mix shift toward higher-margin Penguin Computing solutions and continued SG&A discipline. The balance sheet transformation continues with projected net cash of ~$38M in Q2, a significant improvement from the $62.3M net debt position in Q1.

Key risks that could invalidate this thesis: (1) evidence of customer churn or deal slippage during CEO transition would signal execution problems not yet visible, (2) a material slowdown in hyperscaler AI infrastructure spending would directly impact Penguin Computing, and (3) any reversion to higher GAAP vs adjusted EPS spread would suggest my understanding of the consensus methodology is flawed. The 72% confidence level reflects moderate uncertainty around the exact magnitude of the beat, not the direction - the structural underestimation pattern is well-established.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $0.03 remains 40% below the Wall Street consensus of $0.05, reflecting Richardson Electronics' fundamental structural constraint: the company cannot generate meaningful operating leverage on its fixed SG&A base of approximately $15.7M per quarter. This pattern has been remarkably consistent—Q2 2026 posted a net loss of $0.01 on $52.3M revenue with $15.9M SG&A, while Q1 2026 achieved only $0.13 EPS on stronger $54.6M revenue largely due to favorable non-operating income of $1.4M. The Street appears to be extrapolating from Q1's strong results without recognizing that one-time non-operating gains drove most of that outperformance.

The key data supporting my below-consensus view centers on three immutable facts: (1) SG&A has averaged $15.5-16.0M for the past four quarters regardless of revenue levels between $52-55M, creating zero operating leverage; (2) gross margins remain stuck around 30.7-31.0% with no evidence of product mix improvement; and (3) management has provided no concrete cost reduction initiatives in recent filings. For Q3, I project revenue recovering modestly to $53M as PMT destocking subsides (supported by RFIL's improving semiconductor order commentary), but with SG&A at $15.7M and gross profit at $16.3M, operating income only reaches ~$500K. After minimal interest income and a 30% tax rate, net income approximates $450K or $0.03 per diluted share.

I would reconsider my view if: (1) revenue exceeds $55M, which would create enough gross profit to cover fixed costs and generate meaningful operating income; (2) SG&A drops below $15M through restructuring; or (3) the LaserSlat SAVER product launch generates unexpected traction contributing $1-2M in incremental Q3 revenue. The latter seems unlikely given the March 10 launch date leaves insufficient time for meaningful Q3 contribution. My conviction remains medium—the fixed cost structure is highly predictable, but revenue timing and non-operating items create quarterly volatility.

My Q3 2026 forecast of $0.03 EPS on $108M revenue represents a modest upgrade from my prior $0.02/$106M estimate, reflecting refined analysis of RGP's cost restructuring trajectory. The January 2026 workforce reduction should drive meaningful SG&A savings in Q3 as severance costs were largely absorbed in Q2 (where SG&A spiked to $54.4M). I project Q3 SG&A at $46M, still above the ~$40M target but representing significant sequential improvement. The revenue decline is decelerating - Q2 was down only 2% QoQ versus Q1's sharper drop - suggesting the worst of the demand destruction may be behind us.

My key differentiation from the Street's $0.04 EPS consensus remains a more conservative view on both revenue stabilization timing and the magnitude of near-term cost savings realization. My Q3 FY26 forecast for RPM maintains a SIGNIFICANTLY DIFFERENTIATED view from Wall Street consensus, projecting $0.36 EPS on $1.51B revenue versus consensus of $0.37 EPS on $1.93B revenue. The critical analytical issue remains the ~$420M (22%) revenue gap between my estimate and consensus. RPM's fiscal Q3 (December-February) has ALWAYS been the company's weakest quarter due to construction and coatings seasonality - Q3 FY25 delivered $1.48B revenue with $0.35 EPS (adjusted $0.40 diluted). The Street's $1.93B consensus appears to be either a data anomaly or a confusion with a different fiscal period. My $1.51B estimate represents modest +2% YoY growth, supported by UFP Industries' Q4 showing 7% unit decline (indicating Consumer weakness) and Concrete Pumping Holdings' 5% Q1 revenue growth (indicating stable but not accelerating construction activity).

The key supporting evidence for my thesis includes: (1) Historical seasonal pattern showing Q3 consistently 25-30% below Q1/Q2 revenue levels; (2) Q3 FY25 actual of $1.48B as the comparable base; (3) Third-party indicators from UFP Industries and BBCP aligning with modest growth assumptions; and (4) No management pre-announcement or guidance update suggesting any deviation from seasonal norms. MAP 2025 operational improvements should support ~40bps gross margin expansion YoY to 38.5%, but this cannot overcome the seasonal revenue headwind. The effective tax rate in Q3 is typically minimal or negative due to the seasonal loss pattern, which supports my $0.36 EPS projection.

What would make me change my mind: If RPM releases a pre-announcement indicating unusually strong performance, if I discover the consensus data source is using a different fiscal calendar definition, or if construction leading indicators show acceleration that I've missed. The April 8 earnings release will definitively resolve the consensus discrepancy. My confidence remains elevated at 82% because the seasonal pattern analysis is highly reliable, but I acknowledge the risk that I may be missing information that Street analysts have incorporated into their $1.93B consensus.

My Q4 2026 EPS estimate of $0.51 is $0.02 below consensus of $0.53 and a $0.01 reduction from my previous $0.52 estimate. The primary driver remains accelerating net interest income compression - Q3's NII dropped 17% QoQ from $20.3M to $16.8M as Saratoga's predominantly floating-rate loan portfolio (~$1.1B) continues repricing lower with Fed rate cuts. I project Q4 NII of approximately $14.5-15.0M, representing another 11-14% sequential decline. The $0.75/quarter dividend ($0.25 monthly) announced March 18 confirms management's commitment to maintaining payouts despite a payout ratio now exceeding 130%, which I view as unsustainable.

Wall Street's $0.53 consensus appears to underestimate the velocity of NII compression and the dilutive impact of continued ATM issuance. With cash projected to decline from $52.3M to ~$30M by quarter-end (approaching minimum operating thresholds), and the company continuing to issue equity through ATM programs at depressed prices, both the earnings base and share count work against EPS. The recent $50M 7.25% senior notes provide temporary liquidity but add to interest expense rather than solving the core mismatch between shrinking income and fixed dividend obligations. I see the Street as anchoring too heavily on SAR's historical beat patterns without fully accounting for the structural shift in the rate environment.

Key risks to my thesis include: (1) better-than-expected fee income from new originations that could offset NII weakness, (2) portfolio company realizations generating one-time gains, and (3) a pause in Fed cuts that would slow the compression trajectory. However, the weight of evidence supports continued pressure, and I maintain medium conviction in my below-consensus call.

I am maintaining my below-consensus EPS estimate of ¥38 versus Wall Street's ¥39 consensus for Sugi Holdings Q4 2026, representing a 2.6% negative variance. My conviction in this bearish stance stems from the clear operating margin compression trajectory visible in recent quarters: Q2 2026 operating margin was 5.0% (¥12.68B operating income on ¥254.43B revenue), declining to 4.2% in Q3 2026 (¥10.42B on ¥249.51B). I project this trend to continue into Q4 at approximately 4.0% operating margin, driven by persistent labor cost inflation in Japan and competitive intensity in the drugstore sector requiring promotional activity. This margin compression is the primary driver of my below-consensus view.

The fundamental challenge for Sugi Holdings is balancing growth investments against profitability in a mature, highly competitive Japanese drugstore market. While the pharmacy segment benefits from structural demographic tailwinds (Japan's aging population driving prescription demand), the core drugstore business faces intense competition from Welcia, Tsuruha, and convenience store operators. My revenue estimate of ¥248B assumes modest 1.9% YoY growth driven by pharmacy growth (~3%) partially offset by flat to low-single-digit drugstore performance. Inventory levels remain elevated at approximately ¥103B, creating markdown risk that could further pressure margins.

Critical caveats: My confidence level remains LOW at 0.45 due to severe data quality issues in the available financials. Q1 2026 data shows anomalous figures that appear to be in USD rather than JPY, creating uncertainty in trend analysis. Additionally, no company-specific news has been available for SGIPF - all retrieved articles relate to unrelated companies (SUIG, SGC, SGI). This information vacuum prevents validation or updating of key assumptions. What would change my view: (1) Evidence of margin stabilization through cost rationalization programs, (2) Company-specific news confirming operational improvements, or (3) Better-than-expected pharmacy reimbursement rates.

My Q2 FY2026 estimate of $0.12 EPS on $19.5M revenue reflects high conviction that the stated $0.27 consensus is a stale data artifact completely disconnected from Simulations Plus's current earnings reality. Following the Q3 FY2025 $77.2M goodwill impairment that drove the massive one-time loss, actual quarterly EPS has ranged from -$0.03 to +$0.15, with Q1 FY2026 delivering just $0.03 EPS on $18.4M revenue. The true normalized earning power of this business is $0.08-0.15 per quarter based on the post-impairment cost structure. My $0.12 estimate sits at the upper end of this range, reflecting expected services revenue recovery from $5.7M deferred revenue conversion and R&D expense normalization from Q1's elevated $3.0M to ~$2.5M.

Q1 saw $99.6M in buybacks that increased treasury stock from $129.3M to $230M, retiring approximately 6.3M shares. I estimate diluted shares outstanding have dropped from ~99M in Q1 to approximately 82.5M in Q2, reflecting both the Q1 activity and an additional ~$60M in Q2 repurchases. The Street's consensus likely uses a stale share count assumption in the 90-95M range, which mathematically understates EPS by $0.02-0.03.

The fundamental story is mixed but stabilizing. Quest brand continues to lead the protein bar category with estimated +9% YoY growth, validated by Jefferies' recent upgrade citing the 'protein megatrend.' Atkins remains under pressure from GLP-1 adoption but appears to be stabilizing at -2% YoY rather than accelerating declines. Gross margins should recover from Q1's compressed 32.3% to approximately 33.5% on normalized promotional activity and stable input costs. The Smucker beat earlier this week with 7% sales growth validates consumer staples pricing power remains intact.

Key risk to thesis is share count mechanics - if actual diluted shares come in above 88M, my variant view weakens materially and EPS would be closer to consensus. I'm maintaining medium conviction as the buyback math is relatively transparent and verifiable, but there's uncertainty around the exact timing of repurchases within the quarter. The stock at 52-week lows with institutional accumulation (Landscape Capital +1,420%) suggests the market may be overreacting to margin pressure narratives while missing the buyback accretion story.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $8.65 represents a 68% sequential increase from Q2's $5.15, driven by SanDisk's accelerating transformation into an enterprise AI memory leader. The Wall Street consensus of $13.93 remains fundamentally disconnected from reality - this figure appears to be either an annualized estimate or a data error. Given the company's quarterly progression ($-0.16 in Q4 2025, $0.75 in Q1 2026, $5.15 in Q2 2026), a jump to $13.93 would require an implausible 170% sequential increase. My bottoms-up model shows revenue growing 18.5% QoQ to $3.58B as data center reaches 48% of mix with LTA contracts providing unprecedented visibility and pricing power.

The key differentiated insight driving my bullish-but-not-extreme view is the gross margin trajectory. I'm modeling 53.5% gross margin in Q3 versus 51% in Q2, driven by three factors: (1) BiCS8 technology now comprising over 60% of enterprise shipments with 15%+ cost advantage; (2) LTA contracts locking in favorable pricing while spot market volatility affects competitors; (3) inventory optimization reducing write-downs that plagued earlier quarters. This margin expansion, combined with operating leverage as revenue scales faster than R&D/SG&A, drops significant incremental profit to the bottom line.

The risks I'm monitoring include the March 20 lock-up expiration on 2M shares (near-term stock pressure but no earnings impact), Micron's aggressive capex signaling potential future supply additions, and ongoing SBC dilution at ~3% quarterly rates. My share count assumption of 131M diluted shares reflects the reversal of anti-dilutive effects as profitability increases. The bull case of $9.50+ EPS requires 55%+ gross margins and 20%+ revenue growth; the bear case of $7.00 assumes margin disappointment and China weakness. I'm positioned slightly above the midpoint given LTA contract momentum.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 FY2026 forecast of $2.92 non-GAAP diluted EPS on $15.68B revenue represents a 3.3% discount to Wall Street consensus of $3.02 EPS and 7.5% below consensus revenue of $16.95B. The primary driver of my variant view remains the Street's chronic failure to adequately price seasonal Q4-to-Q1 normalization in TD SYNNEX's distribution business. Historical data shows Q1 revenue declines of 10-15% sequentially as holiday-driven endpoint demand normalizes, yet consensus implies only a 2.5% sequential decline - a pattern that has led to consistent Q1 misses. My 9.8% sequential decline assumption is actually at the conservative end of the historical range.

I've modestly raised my estimate from $2.88 to $2.92 based on two developments: (1) the SCAILIUM AI infrastructure partnership announced February 24, 2026, which provides incremental channel visibility into enterprise AI adoption, and (2) TD SYNNEX's announcement of updated reportable segments including standalone Hyve disclosure, which reduces uncertainty around AI infrastructure contribution. The Cloud Insights UK launch for Microsoft CSP partners also signals continued momentum in Advanced Solutions. However, these positives are partially offset by persistent insider selling (39+:0 buy/sell ratio TTM) and Brave Warrior Advisors' 13.1% stake reduction, suggesting institutional caution.

The key event risk is the March 31 earnings report itself, which will include the first standalone Hyve segment disclosure. If hyperscaler demand is weaker than expected due to inventory digestion, my $900M Hyve estimate could prove too aggressive. Conversely, if AI infrastructure spending has accelerated beyond channel checks, there's upside to my model. I maintain high conviction in the seasonal normalization thesis but acknowledge the Hyve disclosure creates binary risk that could swing results +/- $0.10 from my estimate.

My forecast envisions a 'Profitless Prosperity' scenario for TD Synnex in Q1 2026. I project a Revenue Beat ($17.42B vs Consensus $16.95B) driven by accelerating AI server deployments via Hyve Solutions, consistent with the upstream strength reported by Synopsys. However, I diverge sharply on profitability, forecasting an EPS Miss ($2.85 vs Consensus $3.02). The Street is underestimating the dilutive margin impact of this high-volume, low-margin hyperscale business, which I expect will compress blended gross margins to ~5.75% (comparable to the 6.08% seen in Q1'25 but further pressured by mix).

Key data points supporting this include the massive seasonal Accounts Payable unwind (~$3.7B outflow expectation), which necessitates a significant spike in short-term debt (~$1B+ increase), creating an interest expense headwind ($95M vs $82M last quarter) that consensus hasn't fully priced in. Furthermore, the correlation between upstream design activity (Synopsys) and downstream volume (Hyve) suggests revenue will be 'empty calories' regarding the bottom line.

I would be forced to reconsider this bearish EPS view if the company reports unexpectedly accelerating operating leverage in their core Endpoint Solutions business or if Hyve margins have structurally improved due to value-add services, which would allow the revenue beat to drop through to the bottom line.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of €1.12 (approximately $1.20 at current FX) represents a 3.7% premium to consensus €1.08, driven by underappreciated specialty care momentum and improving pipeline visibility. The Street appears too cautious following the 52-week low share price, but the fundamental transformation story remains intact. Dupixent's triple indication strategy (atopic dermatitis, asthma, COPD) continues to drive double-digit growth, while ALTUVIIIO's blockbuster achievement in 2025 validates the hemophilia franchise pivot. The completion of amlitelimab's COAST 2 Phase 3 trial announced March 19 provides a near-term catalyst that consensus hasn't fully incorporated, potentially positioning Sanofi for a 2026 filing in moderate-to-severe eczema.

The venglustat Breakthrough Therapy Designation for type 3 Gaucher disease adds meaningful pipeline optionality in rare disease, though this contributes no immediate revenue. My differentiated view centers on the quality of Sanofi's revenue mix shift: specialty care now commands higher gross margins (75%+ vs. corporate average 72%) and demonstrates more durable growth characteristics than the declining General Medicines and seasonal Vaccines segments. Q4 2025's 9.9% sales growth and €5.7B new launch revenue confirms this transformation is ahead of schedule.

Key risks to my above-consensus view include: (1) institutional selling pressure continuing despite fundamental strength, (2) unexpected competitive dynamics in the IL-4/IL-13 pathway from emerging OX40L inhibitors, and (3) FX headwinds if EUR strengthens further vs. USD. The 52-week low at $43.32 represents market skepticism I believe is overdone given the 45% implied upside to analyst targets. If Dupixent growth decelerates below 10% YoY or vaccine weakness exceeds seasonal norms by >5 percentage points, I would revisit my above-consensus stance.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 forecast of $2.76 EPS on $4.68B revenue represents a slight upward revision from my prior $2.75 estimate, sitting at the upper half of Steel Dynamics' explicit guidance range of $2.73-$2.77. This positions me 13% BELOW the stale Wall Street consensus of $3.18. The Street has not updated models since tariff-driven optimism in early 2026, and the data clearly shows that tariff benefits have been delayed rather than realized. Steel pricing has remained flat at $775/ton rather than rising toward the $800+ levels bulls anticipated, and management explicitly flagged this timing disconnect in their March 17 guidance release.

The key data points supporting my variant view: (1) Management's March 17 guidance of $2.73-$2.77 was 15% below FactSet consensus of $3.24 at that time - when management itself is guiding materially below Street, the Street is wrong; (2) Hot-rolled coil prices have been stable around $775-780/ton throughout Q1 rather than the $800+ needed to justify consensus; (3) The March 19 news confirming 'higher Q1 earnings on demand and pricing gains' validates the modest sequential improvement but not a dramatic beat scenario; (4) Metals recycling margins are expanding but not enough to offset flat steel spreads.

What would change my view: If pricing data shows a sudden move toward $800/ton in the final weeks of March, or if management revises guidance upward. The Cleveland Cliffs supply disruption (six plants idled) could accelerate pricing in Q2, making my conservative stance more appropriate for Q1 but potentially too bearish for later quarters. My 82% confidence reflects the unusual clarity provided by management's explicit guidance range - they have strong visibility into March shipments and pricing.

The math is straightforward: shares outstanding have declined from 2.60B in Q4 FY25 to 2.44B in Q3 FY26 - a 6.2% reduction in just three quarters. Assuming continued buyback activity at a conservative ¥89B quarterly pace (well below Q3's exceptional ¥162.5B), I project share count declining to approximately 2.38B for Q4, providing meaningful EPS accretion that consensus models appear to underweight.

The revenue outlook of ¥2.475T reflects typical Q4 seasonal strength of 1.8-2.0% sequential growth, supported by healthy North American convenience store demand evidenced by peer results from Kroger and Costco. I'm modeling 26.5% for Q4, which is still above the sub-20% levels seen in Q1-Q2 but reflects some giveback. This is the primary swing factor in my model, with each 100bps of gross margin representing approximately ¥7 in EPS.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence that buyback pace is slowing materially below ¥89B quarterly would reduce my EPS estimate by ¥1-2; (2) If gross margin compresses below 25%, my estimate would need to come down by ¥3-5; (3) Any acceleration in superstore divestiture losses or Couche-Tard-related disruption could impact operating performance. However, absent such developments, I maintain conviction that the Street is underweighting the mechanical EPS benefit from Seven & i's capital return program.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.51 remains 7.3% below Street consensus of $0.55, driven primarily by tax rate normalization that I believe the Street continues to systematically underweight. Q4 2025's reported EPS of $0.52 benefited from an anomalously low 2.6% effective tax rate ($109M on $4.26B pretax income), which management explicitly attributed to discrete tax benefits that are non-recurring. With full-year 2026 ETR guidance of 21%, the Q1 tax expense alone should be ~$966M versus Q4's $109M - an $857M sequential headwind that mathematically compresses EPS by ~$0.12. The consensus appears to be extrapolating from Q4's beat without properly adjusting for this one-time tax benefit.

On the revenue side, I project $30.55B, essentially flat with Q1 2025's $30.63B, reflecting the typical Q1 seasonal decline in equipment sales following the holiday quarter. Equipment revenue should drop approximately 35% sequentially from Q4's elevated levels to around $4.2B, while mobility service revenue continues its steady 2-3% growth trajectory supported by postpaid ARPU improvements and fiber bundling benefits. The March Madness marketing campaign (new spokesperson Ted, expanded AT&T Guarantee) suggests elevated customer acquisition spending, which may pressure SG&A but could support net adds. Fiber net adds should remain around 250K, consistent with the ~1M annual run rate.

The key risk to my below-consensus view is if AT&T realizes additional discrete tax benefits in Q1 similar to Q4. Management has historically been conservative with guidance, and the Street may be pricing in some probability of continued tax favorability. forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 FY2026 forecast of -$0.04 diluted EPS on $372M revenue maintains my conviction that Wall Street's stale -$0.22 consensus is fundamentally broken. The consensus appears anchored to historical periods that included massive non-recurring goodwill impairments ($1.75B in Q4 2025, $1.14B in Q3 2025), while normalized operational performance has demonstrated Tilray achieving near-breakeven for two consecutive quarters (Q1 2026: -$0.003, Q2 2026: -$0.02 adjusted for one-time items). The ~82% delta between my forecast and consensus reflects this fundamental misalignment between historical impairment-laden results and the current operational reality.

The key variant perception driving my thesis is that Tilray has successfully executed a strategic pivot to become a global beverage platform with cannabis optionality. The BrewDog US acquisition (announced March 16-17), Carlsberg partnership (March 3), and Australian medical cannabis expansion (March 19) collectively demonstrate management's execution on the diversification strategy. Q3 2026 will mark the first quarter where beverage contributes over 55% of total revenue (~$210M of $372M), fundamentally changing the risk profile and margin structure of the business. The 4th largest US craft beer position provides stable, recurring revenue with better unit economics than volatile cannabis markets.

However, I've modestly revised my EPS estimate from -$0.03 to -$0.04 to reflect higher-than-anticipated integration costs from the BrewDog US acquisition. The Columbus, Ohio brewery facility and four retail locations require meaningful upfront integration spending that will pressure SG&A in Q3 before scale benefits emerge in Q4 2026+. My conviction remains medium as acquisition integration creates near-term visibility challenges, but the strategic direction is correct. I would revise my thesis bearish if: (1) beverage revenue comes in below $180M suggesting integration problems, (2) cannabis gross margins fall below 30% indicating price war intensification, or (3) management signals need for additional equity raises beyond current ATM program.

The core reason is mix: CC Pharma distribution is the dominant consolidator and tends to anchor quarterly revenue; the recent BrewDog headlines are strategically meaningful but likely contribute little recognized Q3 revenue due to timing, while Australia medical portfolio expansion is more of a demand/positioning signal than an immediate in-quarter revenue step-change.

On earnings, I’m modestly more cautious than my prior EPS view: even if revenue holds, GAAP results can deteriorate on elevated SG&A, stock-based comp, and deal/integration/professional costs. I’m modeling a slightly wider operating loss and a smaller non-operating benefit than Q2, producing EPS of about -$0.30.

I would change my view if filings or subsequent disclosures indicate BrewDog consolidation occurred within Q3 (raising revenue but potentially also costs), or if CC Pharma shows a sharper volume/margin deceleration than implied by the stable consolidated run-rate.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.01 remains 50% below Wall Street's $0.02 consensus, driven by my fundamental disagreement about Tanzania's mining tax regime that the Street continues to underappreciate. The Q1 2026 reported 111% effective tax rate (resulting in net loss despite $17.4M operating income) was NOT an anomaly but reflects structural realities of mining in Tanzania - including 6% production royalties on gross revenue, withholding taxes on gold exports, and deferred tax timing effects. Management's silence on taxes now extends to 29+ days post-February roadshow with no clarity provided at the AGM or in recent filings, suggesting no good news to share on this front.

The key Q2 dynamics show strong production offset by significant ASP headwinds. The March 2 press release confirmed record Q2 production at Buckreef, but gold prices have normalized from Q1's exceptional $3,860/oz realized price to approximately $2,750-2,850/oz - a 26-29% headwind. Combined with 6-7% share dilution from the $21M warrant exercise (approximately 20M new shares), EPS faces meaningful pressure even as revenue grows. I project $38.5M revenue (up 10% QoQ despite ASP decline due to volume gains) with operating income of ~$19M, but effective tax burden near 65% (including royalties and deferred taxes) compresses net income to approximately $3M or $0.01 per diluted share.

What would change my view: Concrete evidence of tax rate normalization (management guidance, auditor commentary, or regulatory changes), sustained gold prices above $3,000/oz, or production significantly exceeding my 14,000 oz estimate. The $21M warrant proceeds creating ~$32M cash position de-risks the balance sheet materially, but doesn't change the structural tax challenge. Until Tanzania tax clarity emerges, I maintain my below-consensus forecast with medium conviction.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.27 represents a 12.5% premium to Street consensus of $0.24, driven by the market's systematic underappreciation of Tesla's transformed business mix. The critical insight is that Energy Storage, which I project at ~$2.9B with 21%+ gross margins, now contributes approximately $0.17-0.18 per share in gross profit - a segment that essentially didn't exist at scale during Q1 2025's disastrous $0.12 EPS print. The Street remains anchored to that disaster quarter and is extrapolating automotive weakness too aggressively while ignoring this structural earnings ballast. Additionally, China February insurance registration data showed encouraging recovery, though I'm tempering enthusiasm given the absence of March delivery figures.

I've adjusted my estimate down slightly from $0.28 to $0.27 to reflect two developments: (1) the NHTSA's intensified FSD probe covering 3.2M vehicles creates potential for a $50-100M remediation reserve that could hit this quarter, and (2) the continued absence of positive European demand signals suggests the region will remain a drag. However, I'm maintaining my above-consensus stance because the energy segment's contribution is verifiable through management commentary and capacity data (Lathrop at full production, UK Ofgem license expansion), and Services growth from the expanding installed base provides another underappreciated earnings stream.

The key risks to my thesis are: (1) March delivery data comes in below 350K, suggesting China recovery was weaker than February indicated, (2) NHTSA probe escalates to require significant reserves this quarter rather than being deferred, or (3) energy segment margins compress due to battery cost pressures. If deliveries come in above 370K, my estimate would likely prove conservative, suggesting upside to $0.29-0.30 EPS.

I would change my mind if Q1 preliminary data shows better-than-expected deposit stability or if management provides guidance indicating NIM has bottomed. Upside risks include faster-than-anticipated loan growth or a sudden easing in funding competition. However, the balance of evidence points to a miss.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $1.17 represents a 3.3% discount to Street consensus of $1.21, driven primarily by two factors the market appears to be underweighting: (1) the dilutive impact of the M&A-driven stock surge on the share count, and (2) incremental M&A advisory and legal costs that will pressure operating margins. The Cintas acquisition announcement at $310/share (representing a 50%+ premium to pre-announcement levels) has materially increased the value of in-the-money stock options and RSUs, which I estimate will push diluted shares to approximately 27.3M from Q1's 18.2M. This is a critical modeling assumption where I believe the Street is lagging.

On the operational side, I project revenue of $628.5M (+4.4% YoY), which is in line with consensus at $620M but reflects continued pricing power and modest volume growth in the core laundry business. However, gross margins will face pressure from persistent labor inflation and energy costs, compressing to approximately 36.2% from Q1's 36.7%. Additionally, the Brodsky & Smith fiduciary duty investigation and ongoing S-4 filing requirements are generating $4-5M in incremental advisory costs that will flow through SG&A. The Q1 2026 EPS miss of -10% revealed that margin challenges are structural, not transitory, and the M&A process only adds complexity.

What would change my view: If the company clarifies that diluted share count calculations will NOT be materially impacted by the M&A premium (perhaps due to treasury stock method adjustments or different option exercise assumptions), my EPS estimate would move significantly higher, potentially above consensus. Additionally, if working capital normalization is stronger than my $18M use assumption, operating cash flow could surprise positively, though this would not directly impact EPS.

The Cintas acquisition ($310/share) was negotiated during this specific quarter (Dec-Feb). Wall Street's consensus is blindly following historical Q2 seasonality (typically UNF's weakest quarter), failing to adjust for this behavioral override.

I would be wrong if transaction-related legal and banking fees are recognized heavily in Q2 GAAP numbers without adjustment, or if management 'cleaned house' by dumping bad inventory/accruals into the quarter before handing over the keys. forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $2.38 is 6.7% above Street consensus of $2.23, reflecting what I believe is a material underestimation of enterprise HDD demand strength and the margin expansion potential from favorable product mix. The massive institutional accumulation over the past week ($50M+ in new positions from Danske Bank, Sherman Portfolios, FNY, and WBI) signals that sophisticated investors are positioning for upside ahead of earnings. More importantly, management's commentary at the Morgan Stanley TMT Conference emphasized that AI storage capacity is 'locked in' with hyperscalers, suggesting forward visibility is stronger than the market appreciates.

The key data points driving my variant view are: (1) Enterprise HDD revenue should reach ~$1.95B, representing 22% YoY growth as AI data center buildouts continue to absorb high-capacity nearline drives; (2) Gross margins should expand to 45.6-45.7% driven by mix shift toward 24TB+ drives with superior economics; (3) The aggressive buyback program (~$600M/quarter) continues to reduce share count, with diluted shares declining to ~375M. The Street appears to be modeling more conservative enterprise growth (~15%) and flat margins, which I believe underestimates the structural shift in WDC's business toward high-margin enterprise storage.

What would change my mind: If channel inventory data shows significant distributor stockpiling (suggesting pull-forward), if Chinese hyperscaler orders are deferred due to geopolitical tensions, or if Seagate reports aggressive pricing actions that pressure industry ASPs. I'm also watching for any signs of AI infrastructure capex slowdown from the major cloud providers in their recent earnings calls. My confidence level is medium-high at 72% given the strong institutional buying signals, but I'm mindful that the 11% stock rally on March 18th may have priced in some of the upside.

Wall Street is mismodeling the seasonality and industrial headwinds for WD-40 in Q2. Consensus revenue of $160M implies sequential growth or defiance of the typical 'winter trough,' which contradicts both historical patterns (where Q2 is the weakest volume quarter) and recent warnings from industrial peers like Donaldson (DCI) and GPC regarding sluggish end-markets. This results in an EPS of $1.48, beating the consensus of $1.39 despite the top-line miss. The 'miss on revenue, beat on earnings' dynamic is classic for high-quality franchises during soft economic patches.

I would revisit this thesis if we saw evidence of a sudden channel inventory restock by major retailers (Home Depot/Lowe's) which could drive a revenue beat, or if oil prices spiked significantly in the quarter (compressing margins). Currently, data points to steady-state operations with tight cost controls.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 WFC EPS estimate of $1.58 represents a modest 1.3% premium to the Street consensus of $1.56, reflecting a view that consensus is slightly underweighting the earnings accretion from Wells Fargo's aggressive capital return program while appropriately pricing in NII headwinds. The key differentiated insight centers on share count dynamics: Wells Fargo has been executing buybacks at a ~$5B quarterly pace, which I estimate will reduce diluted share count to approximately 3.18B from Q4's 3.22B. This provides roughly $0.02-0.03 of incremental EPS support that I believe is systematically underweighted in Street models, which often use static share count assumptions.

On the revenue side, I project total revenues of approximately $31.15B, down 2.1% sequentially from Q4's $31.82B, driven primarily by a ~9.6% decline in net interest income to $11.15B as the lagged effects of 2025 Fed rate cuts continue to compress net interest margins. This is partially offset by resilient non-interest income of approximately $8.70B, supported by wealth management seasonal strength and continued trading volatility. Operating expenses are expected to normalize to ~$13.50B from Q4's elevated $13.98B, as one-time items in SG&A do not recur. The March 6 termination of the 2018 enforcement action remains a positive catalyst for longer-term sentiment, though it does not materially impact Q1 earnings.

What would change my view: If deposit repricing accelerates faster than expected (pushing NII below $11.0B), or if credit quality shows signs of deterioration requiring higher provisions (above $1.2B), I would revise my estimate downward. Conversely, if buyback execution is even stronger than expected or fee income surprises to the upside, there could be additional upside to my estimate.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.68 represents a 6.3% premium to the $1.58 Wall Street consensus, driven by the market's over-anchoring to Q4's weather-impacted miss. The primary driver is the sustained Brent crude environment at $79-81/bbl through mid-March versus Q4's depressed $73/bbl average - this alone provides approximately $2.5B in incremental upstream revenue that consensus has been slow to fully incorporate. The Guyana automated drilling breakthrough announced March 17 represents a structural cost improvement of 8-12% in lifting costs that is not yet priced by the Street, as this technology is just beginning to scale across ExxonMobil's global portfolio.

The downstream segment recovery from Q4's Gulf Coast disruptions provides additional upside. With crack spreads stabilizing at $12-13/bbl and refining throughput normalizing, I project downstream earnings to recover $800M-1B sequentially. The key headwind remains the tax rate normalization from Q4's unusually low 17.7% to a more typical 29%, which I've fully incorporated and which partially offsets the operational improvements. The chemical segment remains challenged by Asian polyethylene oversupply, but this is well-understood and already reflected in depressed estimates.

What would change my view: A meaningful correction in Brent crude below $70/bbl would eliminate the upstream tailwind; a sharper-than-expected crack spread compression would pressure downstream; or evidence that the Guyana automation benefits are slower to materialize than management indicates. The institutional accumulation we've tracked (CIBC's new $67.9M position, Stillwater's $2.87M stake) suggests smart money shares my view that the Q4 miss narrative has created an attractive entry point. My confidence is medium-high given the clear oil price trajectory, though commodity volatility warrants some caution.

My differentiated view versus consensus ($1.58) is that Exxon will report Q1 2026 EPS of $1.54, representing a -2.5% downside surprise. I diverge from consensus by emphasizing that the EIA's 2026 oil price projection, while higher than previous years, is lower than the Street's implicit assumption for Q1, reducing the geopolitical risk premium support to ~$2/bbl vs. prior $2-3/bbl. Concurrently, chemical oversupply and plateauing refining margins are more persistent headwinds than consensus acknowledges, pressuring downstream margins. forecasts.thesis: Consensus EPS $46.39 and absurdly low rev $0.88B (trapped in Q2 anomaly) herds toward industrial slowdown narrative, massively underestimating Yaskawa's robotics dominance in AI/reshoring capex supercycle; we project $152B rev (+12.7% QoQ) on record Q3 $216B inventory priming deliveries, EPS $53 on 12%+ op margins. Key data: peers Kadant record Q4/upbeat '26, Kinaxis record rev, HY materials handling demand strong, Schneider record highs confirm no weakness in automation cycle. Would change mind on major peer misses or Yaskawa pre-announce below Q3 trends.
